title: Betrayal
events_chronological: At a party in his best friend Robert's house, the literary agent Jerry takes Emma upstairs and tells her she is beautiful while the guests drink below.
Jerry and Emma take a flat of their own in a quiet part of the city and furnish it with a tablecloth and crockery so the affair has somewhere domestic to live.
Emma tells Jerry she is expecting a child by Robert, and the two agree that nothing about the flat need change.
In a hotel room in Venice, Robert asks Emma about a letter waiting for her at the poste restante in Jerry's handwriting.
Emma admits the affair, and Robert says only that he has always liked Jerry rather more than he has liked her.
Emma returns to the flat and tells Jerry nothing at all about Venice, and the afternoon passes as every other one has.
Robert drinks his way through a long lunch with Jerry, needling him about modern novels and never once saying what he knows.
At dinner in Robert and Emma's house the two men talk about squash and boys' games until Emma is left out of the conversation altogether.
Jerry and Emma agree that the flat has become a burden, divide the crockery between them and give up the lease.
In a pub two years on, Emma tells Jerry that her marriage is finished and that she sat up the previous night telling Robert everything.
Emma mentions that Robert has been publishing the novelist Casey, whom Jerry represents and whom both men privately despise.
Jerry telephones Robert in a panic and Robert comes round to his house that evening.
Robert tells Jerry he has known about the affair for four years, that Emma told him in Venice, and that he has never much cared for Jerry's letters either.
syuzhet_notes: The nine scenes run from 1977 back to 1968. Told-order bullets 1-2 are the latest thing in the story and bullet 13 the earliest, so every revelation arrives before its cause: the audience learns the affair is over before it learns it began.
fabula_notes: The chronology is fixed by the dates the play prints above each scene. The 1973 scenes play forward among themselves - the hotel confrontation, the flat, the lunch - because each is one continuous scene.
